title: Why Edison Added a Carbon Button
topic: Why Thomas Edison built a “carbon microphone” with a thin carbon button in 1877 to improve telephone signal strength

lines: Thomas Edison slammed a tiny carbon button into his telegraph.
He hoped the speck could carry a voice across town.
His lab mates scoffed, insisting the steel diaphragm was sufficient.
They warned him he’d waste time on a useless gimmick.
Early telephone calls were faint, often disappearing mid‑sentence.
Customers complained they could barely hear each other.
Edison tightened the button, pressed the granules harder, and tried again.
Each tweak made the signal a little louder.
You see, it’s like whispering into a tin can.
When sound hits the thin diaphragm, it squeezes carbon granules.
The pressure lowers the granules’ electrical resistance.
A steady current then varies, creating a strong electric pulse.
That pulse travels the whole line without extra batteries.
That tiny button let phones ring miles on a single wire.
It became the standard for a whole century of telephony.
Even after vacuum tubes arrived, the carbon transmitter still ruled.

claims.claim: Edison filed a patent on a carbon (graphite) transmitter on 27 April 1877.
A carbon microphone uses granules whose pressure‑dependent resistance creates a varying current that reproduces sound.
Carbon transmitters produced much louder signals, letting telephones work over long lines without extra power.
